author: AndersMunch
text:
It’s not the function call. This also triggers RecursionError:
it = [0]
for i in range(5000):
    if i != 2500:
        it = (x+1 for x in it)
    else:
        it = (x+1 for x in it)
print(next(it))

The RecursionError is not surprising. A generator is akin to a little function, and thousands of nested function calls can trigger that.
What’s surprising is that there’s no RecursionError in your first example.
I tried replacing 5000 with 50_000_000. It still runs on 3.14.8.
More data points: Python 3.10.12 triggered RecursionError at the expected depth 1000. Python 3.11.8 crashed.

For something like this, searching those pages for “generator” and “recursion” would be a good start (though I would search for “recursi” so that it also catches “recursive”). I did exactly that, and came up with something in the very earliest version:



Python documentation



sys.setrecursionlimit() - What’s New In Python 3.11
Python frames, holding execution information, are created whenever Python calls a Python function. The following are new frame optimizations: | Editor, Pablo Galindo Salgado,. This article explains the new features in Python 3.11, compared to 3.10....





Now, I can’t say for certain that these generators are getting inlined, but it’s absolutely plausible. You’d have to do further checks to be sure.
Generally speaking, the recursion limit (and RecursionError when you blow past it) is an alternative to outright crashing, rather than being a restriction that you can impose on arbitrary code. If you want to enforce some sort of limit, you may need to look to other tools; it’s possible that audit hooks can do what you want, or maybe spin off a subprocess. But personally, the only reason that I would need to be concerned about this change in behaviour is if I had to support 3.10 and also had something deeply recursive.

author: Stefan2
text:
Anders Munch:

I tried replacing 5000 with 50_000_000. It still runs on 3.14.8.


Makes me yet again wish that Python would finally get rid of the artificial limit. Back when it was there for preventing crashes due to C stack overflow, it was somewhat acceptable. But now that it can do deep recursion without C stack, it’s between annoying and infuriating. One thing I like about Python is that ints simply grow as large as needed, so I don’t have an artificial limit like 32 bits that I need to care about. I wish Python had the same mindset about recursion. Many things are naturally recursive and I want to do them that way, without an artificial limit screwing it up. Recently for example in more-itertools I saw that natural pretty four lines of recursion got replaced by 22 lines of iterative mess. That’s not good.

text:
Stefan Pochmann:

I worry this will get “fixed” by adding a check that then does it for that code, too.


The recursion limit is there to prevent crashes. The reason it isn’t throwing it here is that the calls are being inlined, meaning that there isn’t a limit, and so, there’s no risk of a crash.
If anything changes along those lines, it’s more likely to be other things optimizing away recursion, and thus fewer RecursionErrors.

author: Stefan2
text:
I mean remove RecursionError for cases that don’t post a danger of C stack overflow and crashing Python. That’s the reason the docs provide for the limit:

This limit prevents infinite recursion from causing an overflow of the C stack and crashing Python.

In my understanding, that has been misinformation for a few years now. The C stack is protected with another limit instead. There’s an issue about this, but it was incorrectly closed as a duplicate, and the misinformation persists.
So when some recursion really consumes C stack and that other limit/mechanism detects it, I find a RecursionError acceptable. Although I wish that would be avoided as well, and I imagine if that ever happens, the following generation of coders will find it absurd that we ever did this.
But when some recursion doesn’t consume C stack, then the documented reason for the existence of the limit we can get/set with sys doesn’t even apply, so I wish that those cases wouldn’t raise that error. Leave my perfectly fine recursion alone, and if I do make a mistake and cause infinite recursion, I expect a MemoryError.
